title: "Internal audits and management review"
order: 25

## The ticket

Three weeks after your Quality Analyst's FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) scored
the tracked-distribution-and-acknowledgment process, the audit it set up is done. Using
`quality-risk-management`'s risk ranking and filtering — sites sorted into high, medium,
and low bins by turnover, volume, and time since last review — her team checked
downtime-readiness at the four high-priority satellite sites first.

Three came back clean. The fourth, Lakeshore's Fairview collection site, didn't. The site
lead's signed, dated acknowledgment of the current downtime SOP (standard operating
procedure) revision was on file, right where module 4's tracked-distribution process
expects it. But when the auditor actually opened the binder, it still held the *previous*
revision. The acknowledgment was real. The swap never happened.

Your QA catches your eye before you can say anything. "That's failure mode five. The one
the FMEA ranked above the one we already lived through." She's right — RPN
(Risk Priority Number) 50, "acknowledgment on file, binder never actually swapped," the
risk a formal process surfaced that nobody's war story would have found. It just stopped
being a hypothetical.

"I'm opening this the same way I opened Owen Pruitt's," she says. "Discovery today,
containment first, extent-of-condition next — how many other sites have a real binder
that doesn't match their acknowledgment — then disposition and a CAPA (corrective and
preventive action) call. It just started in an audit instead of a reconciliation report."

That instinct is exactly right, and it's the first half of what this module teaches. The
second half shows up two days later, when she hands you the draft packet for next week's
quarterly management review — the standing meeting where Lakeshore's executive and
quality leadership look at the whole quality system, and where you're expected to sit in
as the system owner for everything IT-adjacent. It reads clean:

> *Internal audit: 4 sites reviewed, 1 finding, corrective action initiated.*
> *CAPA log: 5 closed this quarter, 3 open.*
> *Change control: 12 changes processed, no overdue verifications.*
> *Risk management: FMEA on file for the distribution process.*

Every line is true. Every line is also, on its own, almost useless. Nothing here says
whether the finding count is rising or falling, whether any of those five "closed" CAPAs
closed on real effectiveness data or just on "the fix shipped," or whether anyone with
authority actually decided to do anything differently because of what's in this packet.
Before you sit in that room, you have to know the difference between a packet that
*looks* complete and one that actually shows a quality system working. That's this
module's whole job.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

Start with the failure mode both halves of this module exist to prevent. A quality
system that never independently checks whether real practice matches its own documented
requirements drifts, quietly, until an outside party — an AABB (American Association of
Blood Banks) assessor or an FDA investigator — finds the gap first, at the worst possible
moment: during an inspection, with a citation attached. Internal assessment is Lakeshore's
own early-warning system, run on its own schedule, before anyone else is watching.

And a quality system that only ever looks at findings one at a time never sees the
pattern underneath them. One finding — a binder that didn't get swapped — looks like
noise. Four findings like it across a year, each closed individually and never looked at
together, is signal: a mechanism with a real, recurring weak point. Nobody at the
finding-by-finding level is positioned to see that. Someone has to periodically pull back
and look at the whole system's performance at once. That's management review's entire
reason to exist, and it's why this module — not the QA's audit work, but what leadership
does with what the audit (and everything else this course taught) produces — is squarely
your altitude, not just hers.

You already run both halves of this, under different names. **Internal audit** is your
own internal service review or compliance check: the exercise of going and confirming
that a process actually runs the way its documentation says it does, instead of assuming
it does because nobody's complained. If you've sat through an ISO 20000 or ISO 27001
internal audit, or run a SOX-style internal control test, you've done this exact motion —
independent eyes checking practice against paper, on a schedule, whether or not anything
looks broken.

**Management review** is your quarterly governance board or executive service review —
ITIL 4 names this loop "evaluate, direct, monitor": leadership periodically steps back
from ticket-by-ticket firefighting to look at aggregate metrics — SLA (service-level
agreement) trend lines, major-incident counts, backlog aging — and makes resourcing and
policy calls at the system level. The bridge holds all the way through, with one test
that decides whether either practice is real or theater, in both worlds: **did the
meeting produce documented decisions and resource commitments, or did it produce a status
readout everyone nodded at?** A governance board that only ever reviews slides and never
approves a budget line or kills a bad process is exactly Q9's "risk assessment that lives
only in someone's head" from the last module, wearing an executive calendar invite instead
of a whiteboard.

## The process in plain English

Two related practices, and this course closes by showing how they connect to everything
that came before.

**Internal assessment — QSE (Quality System Essential) 8, Assessments: Internal and
External**, module 1's eighth drawer. Structurally, it's a **planned, periodic,
independent** look at whether Lakeshore's actual practice matches what its documents say
it should be doing. Three words carry the weight:

- **Planned** — scheduled in advance, the way module 6's risk ranking decided which sites
  get checked first, not triggered only when something already looks wrong.
- **Periodic** — run on a defined interval, so drift gets caught on a schedule instead of
  by luck.
- **Independent** — the person checking the work isn't the person who did it. AABB's
  public framework names auditor independence explicitly. This module states that fact
  and stops there — *how* Lakeshore builds and staffs an independent audit program
  (who qualifies as independent, how auditors get trained and assessed for competence,
  how a schedule gets built, how evidence gets sampled) is a full course of its own,
  named below. Here, independence is a property the audit has to have, not a skill this
  lesson teaches you to design.

You'll meet two shapes of internal audit in practice. A **system or process audit**
checks one process across many instances — exactly what Fairview's team just ran,
checking downtime-readiness across several sites. A **tracer audit** runs the opposite
direction: it follows one specific unit from donor to final disposition and checks every
control it should have passed through along the way. If Lakeshore ever ran a tracer audit
on Owen Pruitt's donation, it would retrace donor eligibility, collection, testing,
quarantine, release, and distribution — the exact path `deviations-and-nonconformances`
already walked you through, checked step by step instead of reconstructed after the fact.

Here's the connection this module exists to make explicit, and it's the most important
sentence in this section: **an internal audit finding is not a separate kind of problem
with its own process. It is a deviation, discovered through a different channel, and it
runs through the exact same five stages `deviations-and-nonconformances` already taught
you** — discovery, containment, impact and extent assessment, disposition, and a
documented CAPA decision. Module 2 named several ways a deviation gets discovered
(routine reconciliation, a complaint, a monitoring alarm, self-report). Internal audit is
simply one more entry point into that same machinery, not a parallel track with looser
rules. Fairview's binder finding gets a discovery date (the day the auditor opened the
binder), containment (pull the superseded revision, confirm the current one goes in
today), an extent-of-condition check (does the same acknowledgment-without-swap gap exist
at any other site, including the three that passed this round), a disposition, and a
CAPA decision — reasoned exactly the way module 3 taught, not waved through because "we
found it ourselves and it's already basically fixed."

**Management review — largely QSE 1, Organization**, module 1's first drawer, the one
that also owns executive accountability for the quality system as a whole. Structurally,
it's a **defined, periodic** review — quarterly is typical, but the specific cadence is
Lakeshore's own policy choice, not a number this lesson invents — by organizational
leadership, using **specific inputs** to produce **specific outputs**. This is where
every module in this course lands:

**Inputs**, all of them things this course's earlier modules already produce:

- Internal (and external) audit results — not just a finding count, but what happened to
  each finding.
- Deviation and CAPA trends: how many, what kind, and — critically — CAPA **aging**,
  because an overdue CAPA backlog is itself a finding, per module 3.
- CAPA effectiveness data specifically: closures backed by a passed effectiveness check
  (module 5's clean six-month audit), not just "implemented."
- Change control metrics: volume, on-time implementation and verification, per module 4.
- Risk assessment outputs: FMEA results, accepted risks and their reasoning, and whether
  scheduled risk reviews actually happened, per module 6.
- Complaints and training status, named by AABB's framework as inputs too, in one line —
  not built out further here.

**Outputs**, and this is the half a superficial packet skips: **resourcing decisions**
(more audit staff, a budget line for the automated review-date trigger module 3 left
unbuilt and module 6's FMEA flagged again), **policy or process changes** (tightening the
document-control audit to always include a physical binder check, the exact fix module 6
proposed for failure mode 5), and a **documented judgment**, signed by leadership, on
whether the quality system is effective as a whole. A management review that produces a
set of approved minutes with none of these three things in it hasn't actually happened,
whatever the meeting invite said.

This is squarely where you sit. Auditing isn't your job — your QA and her team do that.
But management review is a leadership function, and as the owner of the systems several
of this course's inputs run on (the tracked-distribution mechanism, BECS's reconciliation
process), you're one of the people this meeting expects real input and real decisions
from — not just a seat in the room.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(c) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph c" | A thorough investigation, including conclusions and followup, of any discrepancy shall be made and recorded. Already quoted in full in `risk-and-controls-vocabulary` and reused in modules 2 and 6. | The same regulatory floor under Fairview's finding as under Owen Pruitt's — a thorough, recorded investigation, regardless of which channel discovered the discrepancy. |

That's the whole table, and that's deliberate, not an oversight — see below.

## The actual text

This module has almost no new regulatory text, for the same reason `capa-root-cause-to-
effectiveness`, `change-control-for-regulated-systems`, and `document-control-and-records`
each found before it: this course's earlier full-text search of Part 606 (run while
scoping the course, and not contradicted by anything found while drafting this module)
turned up no occurrence of "audit," "management review," or "self-inspection" anywhere in
Part 606's regulatory text. Neither internal assessment nor management review is named by
FDA's blood-manufacturing regulation. What Part 606 requires is the same investigation
standard every deviation in this course has already had to satisfy, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.100.md`:

> A thorough investigation, including the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained
> discrepancy or the failure of a lot or unit to meet any of its specifications shall be
> made and recorded.

Read that against Fairview's binder finding specifically: the regulation doesn't care
*how* the discrepancy was discovered — a routine data-entry catch, a hospital complaint,
or an internal auditor opening a binder are all equally "an unexplained discrepancy," and
all equally owe Lakeshore a thorough, recorded investigation. That's the regulatory floor
underneath the "same process, different entry point" point this whole module makes.

The structured practices built on top of that floor — a scheduled, independent internal
audit program, and a periodic management review with defined inputs and outputs — are
AABB's Quality Systems Framework, not Part 606's text. Assessments: Internal and External
(QSE 8) is where AABB places internal audit; management review sits under Organization
(QSE 1), the same drawer that owns executive accountability for the whole quality system.
Both are binding on Lakeshore through AABB accreditation, the same tier every "this isn't
in Part 606's words" finding in this course has landed on for CAPA, change control, and
document control.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

Two different artifacts, for two different practices, and a gap in either is a real
finding on its own.

**For internal audit**, evidence it actually happens on schedule, with findings that go
somewhere. An audit calendar with dates that were kept, a completed audit report per
cycle — not "the schedule says we do this," but records showing it was done — and, for
every finding, a trail leading into the deviation/CAPA system: a discovery date, a
disposition, a CAPA decision with reasoning. An audit program that produces findings that
disappear into a spreadsheet nobody else reads is functionally the same gap as a deviation
record that never reaches a reportability determination.

**For management review**, evidence the meeting produced something. Minutes showing who
attended (the right leadership, not just Quality), the specific inputs actually reviewed
(not "quality metrics were discussed" — which metrics, with what trend), and — this is
the tell an assessor reads fastest — **documented decisions and resource commitments tied
to dates and owners**, not a summary of what was said. "Management review occurred" with
an attendance sheet and nothing else is close to worthless as evidence; "management
review decided to fund an automated document-control review-date trigger, owner assigned,
target date set" is exactly what the practice is supposed to produce.

## Common traps

**"Management review is just a status update meeting."** The single most common failure
of this practice, and the one this module's opening scenario is built around. A packet
full of accurate counts — findings closed, CAPAs closed, changes processed — is a status
report. Management review isn't finished until it has produced a documented decision:
resources committed, a policy changed, or an explicit, signed judgment that the system is
effective as-is. A meeting that reviews the same three bullet points every quarter with no
decision attached to any of them hasn't been doing management review; it's been reading
the packet out loud.

**Treating an internally-found deviation more leniently than one an outsider caught.**
"We found this ourselves, during our own audit, so it's not as serious" is a real and
tempting instinct, and it's exactly backwards from what an assessor expects. A finding
discovered through internal audit gets the *same* discovery-to-CAPA process as one a
hospital complaint or a routine reconciliation catch would trigger — same containment
urgency, same extent-of-condition rigor, same reportability test if it applies. An
assessor who sees an audit-log entry get a softer, faster, less-documented path than an
externally-triggered deviation reads that as exactly what it is: a double standard that
undermines the credibility of the internal audit program itself.

**A packet that lists metrics without analyzing them.** "5 CAPAs closed, 3 open" is a
count. "5 closed, all with passed effectiveness checks; 3 open, average age 40 days,
trending down from last quarter's 65" is analysis — the same finding count, turned into
something a decision can actually be based on. The gap between these two sentences is the
entire difference between a management-review packet that shows a working system and one
that just shows someone kept a tally.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask for the trend, not the count.** "How many findings this cycle" tells you almost
  nothing on its own. "Is that number rising, falling, or flat against the last three
  cycles, and why" is the question a working management review has already answered
  before you walk into the room.
- **Check that "closed" means closed on effectiveness data, not on "the fix shipped."**
  Module 3 taught you this distinction once already; a management-review packet is where
  it matters most, because it's easy for a summary slide to quietly collapse "implemented"
  and "proven effective" into the same word.
- **Watch for a double standard between audit-discovered and externally-discovered
  findings.** If an internal-audit finding is moving faster, with less documentation, than
  a comparable deviation caught some other way, that gap is itself worth raising — before
  an assessor raises it for you.
- **Come to management review with your own inputs prepared, not just an opinion.** As
  the owner of the systems several of this course's inputs run through, you're expected to
  bring real numbers — change-control metrics, risk-review status on anything you own — not
  just react to what Quality presents.
- **Leave the meeting with something written down.** If management review didn't produce a
  documented decision, a resourcing commitment, or an explicit effectiveness judgment with
  your name or your budget attached to at least one line, ask what the meeting actually
  decided before you sign off that it happened.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "Management review is an FDA requirement for every blood establishment — Part 606 requires it." True or false?

False, and it's this module's designated version of a pattern the whole course has taught:
Part 606's text never uses the phrase "management review," the same way it never named
CAPA, change control, or document control. This course's earlier full-text search of Part
606 found no occurrence of "audit," "management review," or "self-inspection" anywhere in
its regulatory text. Management review is an AABB Standards requirement, under the
Organization QSE — binding on Lakeshore because it holds AABB accreditation, enforced
through assessment, not FDA inspection. Tell your CIO: the law requires a thorough,
recorded investigation of any discrepancy, whoever finds it and however it's found; AABB's
Standards are what require leadership to periodically step back and judge the whole system
against everything that investigation work has produced.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your QA says, "We found the Fairview binder gap ourselves during an internal audit, so it doesn't need the full deviation process the way Owen Pruitt's event did — we can just log it as a quick audit note and fix it." Reasonable?

No. An internal audit finding is a deviation discovered through a particular channel, not
a lighter-weight category of problem. It owes the same discovery date, containment,
extent-of-condition check, disposition, and documented CAPA decision as any other
deviation — regardless of who found it or how routine the finding felt in the moment.
Treating an audit-sourced finding more leniently than an externally-discovered one is
exactly the double standard this module's common traps section names, and it's one of the
fastest ways to undermine an assessor's confidence in the audit program itself: if internal
audit findings get a shortcut, why would anyone trust the audit program to surface the
ones that matter?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The management-review packet says "CAPA log: 5 closed this quarter, 3 open." Is that enough for a director to judge whether Lakeshore's quality system is actually working?

No — it's a count, not an analysis, and this module's whole finish line is learning to
tell the difference. A working management-review input would say how many of those five
closures had a passed effectiveness check behind them (versus just "implemented"), what
the three open CAPAs' aging looks like against Lakeshore's own targets, and whether that
trend is improving or worsening compared to prior quarters. A packet that stops at the raw
count looks complete and tells you almost nothing you could act on — which is exactly the
gap between a management-review packet that shows a system working and one that just shows
someone kept score.
:::

## Where this goes next

This closes `quality-system-essentials`. One event — a stale deferral list, a superseded
downtime binder, a unit that shipped before anyone caught it — ran the whole machinery
this course built, module by module: a deviation taken from discovery through a documented
reportability call, a CAPA that found a real system cause and proved its fix worked, a
change controlled through impact assessment and verified implementation, a document-control
process that finally keeps the wrong version out of the building, a formally scored risk
assessment, and now an internal audit whose finding ran through that same deviation machinery
one more time — feeding a management review built to turn all of it into resourcing
decisions and a real judgment about whether the system works.

Two places to go from here. `fda-and-aabb-in-practice`, the next course in this track, is
where the audit-program design work this module deliberately left alone lives: auditor
independence and competency, building an actual audit schedule, evidence sampling,
nonconformance grading — plus facing an FDA inspection or AABB assessment directly,
Form 483 observations, and what a recall or a Warning Letter actually means. It isn't
built yet. And if what you want next is sharper at reviewing your own QA's work
product — her deviation write-ups, her CAPA effectiveness checks, her audit findings,
closely enough to catch what an inspector would catch before it leaves your building —
that's `directing-the-quality-analyst`, also not yet built, and the course this
curriculum's own sequencing recommends you take next.
